passage: Ms Nair's class was doing fractions on the board. Pooja wasn't sure of the answer, but her hand went up anyway. “Three-sixths?” she said. “Not quite,” said the teacher, smiling, “but let's see how you got there.” Pooja explained, and the teacher wrote her steps on the board. “Look, Pooja found half the puzzle. Who can find the rest?” A boy giggled at the back. “We all learn by being wrong,” the teacher said mildly, and the giggle stopped. Abhinav, who never spoke in class, kept his hand low, though his eyes followed the chalk. Three more hands went up.

qa.q: What fraction did Pooja offer as her answer?
qa.a: Pooja offered “Three-sixths?” as her answer.

qa.q: Why did Pooja raise her hand even though she was not sure of the answer?
qa.a: Pooja seems to feel safe being wrong in this room, because mistakes here are treated as part of learning. 🙂

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped children keep volunteering?
qa.a: The teacher asked how Pooja got there, wrote her steps on the board, and stopped the giggle mildly while calling wrong answers a way to learn.

qa.q: What might Abhinav be thinking as his eyes follow the chalk while his hand stays low?
qa.a: Abhinav may be interested and slowly gaining trust that a wrong answer will be safe, but is not ready yet to speak.

grounding: A child in a warm classroom raises a hand though unsure because mistakes are treated as part of learning.

passage: I'm Harsha, and I sit two rows behind Harish. Harish hadn't put a hand up all term. Today the teacher asked what one-half plus one-quarter was, and Harish's hand went up slowly. “Two-sixths?” he said. I held my breath. Nobody laughed. The teacher wrote it on the board and said, “That's a very useful mistake. It shows us what happens when we add the bottoms.” Harish's ears turned red. I can't tell what he felt. But when the next question came, his hand went up again, a bit faster.

qa.q: Where does Harsha sit compared with Harish?
qa.a: Harsha sits two rows behind Harish.

qa.q: What might Harish have been feeling when Harish's ears turned red?
qa.a: Harish may have felt exposed and shy after speaking, though Harsha can't be sure. The hand going up faster for the next question suggests the moment felt safe enough.

qa.q: What could the teacher do next to keep Harish volunteering?
qa.a: The teacher could keep treating mistakes as useful, call on Harish when a hand goes up and praise the effort, not just the right answer.

qa.q: How might Harsha have felt watching Harish's hand go up again?
qa.a: Harsha, who had held a breath in case anyone laughed, probably felt relieved and glad for Harish when the hand rose faster the second time.

grounding: An observer watches a child who never volunteered answer unsure in a class where mistakes are treated as part of learning.

passage:
'Who can tell me why the ice cube melted faster on the steel plate?' asked Mrs Das.
Jahnavi's hand went halfway up, then stopped.
'Go on, Jahnavi. Half an idea is welcome here.'
'Because... steel is colder?'
Tarun giggled. Mrs Das didn't look at him. 'Interesting. Steel feels colder, doesn't it? Who thinks something else?'
Tarun said, 'Steel passes heat faster?'
'Yes! And Jahnavi's answer helped us get there, because it's what most people think. A great wrong answer.'
Jahnavi grinned. 'So steel only feels cold because it takes heat from my hand?'
'Exactly.'
Later, when Mrs Das asked about wooden spoons, Jahnavi's hand shot straight up.

qa.q: Where did the ice cube melt faster?
qa.a: On the steel plate.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi's hand going only halfway up suggest?
qa.a: Jahnavi was unsure and a little nervous about being wrong in front of the class.

qa.q: How did Mrs Das make it safe to be wrong?
qa.a: She welcomed 'half an idea', ignored the giggle, and showed how Jahnavi's wrong answer helped the class reach the right one.

qa.q: What is it like for Tarun when Mrs Das doesn't react to his giggle?
qa.a: His giggle gets no attention, so the laughing fades, and he joins in by offering his own idea.

grounding: A child in a warm classroom raises a hand while unsure, because a wrong answer is treated as useful.

passage: In Class 5, I was the kid who never put a hand up. Then Omkar sir came to teach maths. On the first day he wrote a sum on the board, got it wrong on purpose, and waited. Lalit spotted it first. Sir said, 'Thank you! Mistakes are how we find the right way.' After that, whenever someone answered wrong, sir asked, 'What were you thinking?' and usually found something right inside it. Nobody laughed, because sir never did. One day I put my hand up for a fraction question, not sure at all. I said three-fifths. It was three-eighths. Sir said, 'Good, you knew the top part. Now let's fix the bottom.' That's how I, Tanvir, started talking in class.

qa.q: What did Omkar sir do on the first day?
qa.a: He wrote a sum on the board, got it wrong on purpose, and waited.

qa.q: How was Tanvir feeling when raising a hand for the fraction question?
qa.a: Tanvir felt unsure and nervous, not sure at all of the answer, yet safe enough to try.

qa.q: What could other teachers borrow from Omkar sir?
qa.a: Asking 'What were you thinking?' after a wrong answer and pointing out the part that was right, so children keep trying.

qa.q: How might Lalit have felt when sir thanked Lalit for spotting the mistake?
qa.a: Lalit probably felt proud and encouraged, seeing that catching errors was welcomed.

grounding: A child who never answered starts raising a hand once a teacher treats mistakes as part of learning.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 3B, Monday. Rashmi, who joined us from another school in June, had not answered a single question aloud in three weeks. Today, in our reading circle, she raised her hand to guess what 'enormous' meant. She said 'very noisy'. A few children started to smile; Chandrika whispered, 'Remember our rule,' and they stopped. I thanked Rashmi, said noisy things are often enormous, like thunder, and asked the class to help her finish the idea. Chandrika offered 'very big'. Rashmi nodded, smiling. In maths she raised her hand twice more. I will pair Rashmi with Chandrika for this week's reading, and I'll mention the brave guessing to her mother at pickup today.

qa.q: What guess did Rashmi give for 'enormous'?
qa.a: 'Very noisy'.

qa.q: What does Rashmi raising her hand twice more in maths suggest?
qa.a: She felt safer and more confident after her wrong guess was treated kindly.

qa.q: What did the teacher plan next to build on today?
qa.a: Pairing Rashmi with Chandrika for this week's reading and mentioning the brave guessing to her mother at pickup.

qa.q: How might Chandrika see her part in the reading circle?
qa.a: Chandrika seems to feel responsible for the class rule, gently stopping the smiles and then helping finish Rashmi's idea.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a quiet new child daring to guess aloud once the class treats a wrong answer kindly.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today in maths Trisha Ma'am asked what seven times eight is. I wasn't sure. My hand went up anyway, half up, like it was scared too. I said fifty-four. Wrong! But nobody laughed. Ma'am said, "Thank you, Swati, that's a brave guess. Who can help us check it?" Farhan came to the board and we counted the sevens together, all the way to fifty-six. Ma'am wrote "Mistakes show us the way" next to it. Last year in Sir's class I never put my hand up, not even once. Today I put it up three times and got two right. My tummy didn't do the flippy thing at all.
Swati 🙂

qa.q: What answer did Swati give for seven times eight?
qa.a: Swati said fifty-four.

qa.q: How can you tell that Swati felt less nervous today than last year?
qa.a: Swati's tummy didn't do the flippy thing and the hand went up three times, which shows feeling calm and safe instead of scared.

qa.q: What could other teachers learn from how Trisha Ma'am handled the wrong answer?
qa.a: Thanking the child and asking the class to check together turns a mistake into shared work, so children keep trying.

qa.q: How might Farhan have felt on being asked to help check the answer?
qa.a: Farhan was probably pleased to be useful, and learned that in this class you help with a mistake instead of laughing at it.

grounding: Swati's diary shows a child in a warm class raising a hand even when unsure, because mistakes are treated as part of learning.
